stem: An incident report opens with a short section written for the board and senior managers. What is this section called?

options.text: Technical appendix
Evidence inventory
Chain-of-custody form
Executive summary

explanation: The executive summary translates the incident into business impact and status for leadership. A technical appendix holds detail for responders, an evidence inventory lists collected items, and a chain-of-custody form records who handled evidence.

stem: What is the main purpose of formally declaring a security incident?

options.text: To activate the response plan and its team
To remove the related alerts from the analyst queue
To notify every customer about the event right away
To start the lessons learned meeting for the team

explanation: Declaration is the point where analysis is confirmed as an incident and the response team and plan are activated. It does not clear alerts, it does not by itself trigger customer notices, and lessons learned come after the incident is closed.

stem: A Tier 1 analyst confirms that ransomware is encrypting file servers in several business units. Which severity and escalation path fits best?

options.text: Low, handled by the Tier 1 analyst without escalation
Medium, queued for review during the next scheduled shift
Critical, bringing in executives and key support teams
Informational, recorded in the log with no further action

explanation: Widespread encryption of business systems is a critical incident, and critical incidents go to executives and supporting teams. Low and medium severities stay with lower tiers, and an informational rating would underplay confirmed damage.

stem: Which approach to an after-action review best encourages honest input from the responders?

options.text: Naming the analyst whose mistake started the incident for the record
Keeping it blame-free and focused on process and systems
Limiting attendance to the managers who were on call
Scheduling it a year later during the next audit

explanation: A non-punitive review focused on process and decisions lets people speak openly about what went wrong. Naming individuals discourages candor, excluding responders removes the people who know what happened, and waiting a year loses detail.

stem: During a root cause analysis, a team asks "why" after each answer until it reaches a process gap, such as a missed patch review. Which method is this?

options.text: Fishbone analysis
Five Whys
Fault tree analysis
Timeline causal analysis

explanation: The Five Whys method repeats the question iteratively to move from the symptom to the base cause. A fishbone sorts causes into categories, a fault tree maps branching failures, and timeline analysis orders causes and effects chronologically.

stem: A team lists contributing causes under the branches people, process and technology on a diagram shaped like a skeleton. Which root cause method is this?

options.text: Five Whys questioning of the owner
Fault tree analysis of failures
Kill chain mapping of attacker stages
Ishikawa (fishbone) analysis

explanation: The fishbone, or Ishikawa, diagram places the incident at the head and groups possible causes along category branches. Five Whys is a single chain of questions, a fault tree is a branching failure map, and kill chain mapping describes attacker stages, not causes.

stem: Mail systems may be compromised during an incident. How should the response lead coordinate with the team?

options.text: Use an out-of-band channel such as a phone bridge
Keep using corporate email but encrypt every message
Post updates in the comments of the shared ticket
Use the same mail system but leave out personal names

explanation: When primary systems may be compromised, an out-of-band channel keeps response traffic away from the attacker. Encrypting mail the attacker can read in a mailbox does not help, ticket comments live on a system that may be affected, and omitting names does not hide content.

stem: A customer notice about a data incident should include which of the following?

options.text: The internal hostnames of the affected servers
The detection rule that raised the first alert
What data was affected and what the customer should do next
The names of the analysts who worked the case

explanation: External audiences get limited information: what happened to their data and the actions they can take. Hostnames, detection logic and staff names are internal details that help attackers or create legal and privacy exposure.

stem: An analyst finds that employee health records were copied out of a database. Who should be brought in early to decide on any notification duties?

options.text: The help desk team lead on call
The facilities manager for the site
Legal and compliance personnel
The marketing department leadership

explanation: Legal and compliance staff know which regulations and contracts apply and who must be told, and by when. The help desk, facilities and marketing do not set notification obligations.

stem: A SOC measures the average time between the start of malicious activity and the alert that identifies it. Which metric is this?

options.text: Mean time to respond
Mean time to detect
Mean time to remediate
Mean time to close

explanation: Detection time runs from the start of the activity to its identification. The other metrics measure what happens after detection: the response, the removal of the root cause, and the full closure of the record.

stem: A quarterly report shows that the average time to remove the underlying cause of incidents and verify the fix is rising. Which metric is increasing?

options.text: Mean time to detect threats
Alert volume over the quarter
Mean time to close tickets
Mean time to remediate

explanation: Mean time to remediate tracks how long it takes to eliminate the root cause and restore systems after containment. Detection time measures discovery, alert volume counts alerts, and time to close ends only after the record is documented.

stem: A SOC lead wants one number for end-to-end handling, from alert creation until the ticket is fully closed and documented. Which metric fits?

options.text: Mean time to close
Mean time to detect
Phishing click rate
False positive rate

explanation: Mean time to close covers the whole lifecycle through documentation. Detection time covers only discovery, and phishing click rate and false positive rate are not time measures.

stem: Alert volume doubled after a new detection tool was added, but confirmed incidents stayed flat. What does the trend most likely indicate?

options.text: More noise that needs tuning to reduce false positives
Better coverage proven by more incidents
Attackers have stopped targeting the company
Analysts are closing cases more quickly

explanation: Rising alerts with no rise in confirmed incidents points to noise, which causes fatigue and calls for tuning. More incidents would be needed to show better coverage, and nothing in the data suggests fewer attackers or faster analysts.

stem: A detection rule stays silent while a real intrusion is under way. How is this result classified?

options.text: True positive
False positive
False negative
True negative

explanation: A missed real event is a false negative, the result that worries SOC managers most because no alert is raised. A true positive is a correct alert, a false positive is an alert on benign activity, and a true negative is silence when nothing is wrong.

stem: The security team compares the share of employees who clicked a simulated phishing link before and after a training campaign. What does this metric mainly show?

options.text: How noisy the mail gateway alerts are
How effective awareness training is
How quickly incidents are remediated
How many true positives the SIEM raised

explanation: A falling click rate indicates that training is changing behavior. It says nothing about alert noise, remediation speed or SIEM detections.

stem: A KPI dashboard counts incidents, but analysts rate severity differently from shift to shift. Which KPI problem does this show?

options.text: High storage cost for log data
Too few detection tools in use
Slow ingestion of logs into the SIEM
Subjectivity in classifying and counting incidents

explanation: When classification depends on the person, counts and trends are inconsistent. Storage cost, tool count and ingestion delay are real log or tooling issues but do not explain inconsistent severity ratings.

stem: At the end of a shift, an analyst writes up open cases, pending actions and current severities for the incoming team. Which document is this?

options.text: An after-action report
A shift turnover report
An executive summary
A threat intelligence bulletin

explanation: A turnover report hands over the operational picture so work continues without gaps. An after-action report reviews a closed incident, an executive summary briefs leadership, and a bulletin shares adversary information.

stem: After an incident, the team publishes a report that maps the adversary tactics and techniques seen to a common framework so detection engineers can tune rules. Which report is this?

options.text: Internal threat intelligence report
A shift turnover report for analysts
An executive summary for the board
A compliance attestation for auditors

explanation: Internal threat intelligence reports turn what was observed during incidents into tactics, techniques and indicators for defenders. Turnover reports hand over cases, executive summaries brief leadership, and attestations confirm compliance.

stem: Which part of a post-incident report records the work that remains, with an owner and a due date for each item?

options.text: Incident timeline
Scope statement
Evidence inventory
Follow-up actions

explanation: Follow-up actions list the residual risk work and who will do it by when. The timeline orders what happened, the scope statement says what was affected, and the inventory lists collected evidence.

stem: Which sentence belongs in an executive summary rather than in the technical section of an incident report?

options.text: A scheduled task named updater was created on ws-0412.example.internal by the intruder.
Packet captures show 4,200 connection attempts to TCP port 445.
Orders were down three hours; containment is done and recovery is under way.
The dropped file hash matched a sample seen in earlier incidents.

explanation: Executives need impact and status in plain language. Task names, connection counts and file hash matches are technical findings that belong in the detailed sections.

stem: Counsel says a breach of cardholder data creates duties to notify the card brands and the acquirer. What should decide who is notified and when?

options.text: The severity label first assigned by the Tier 1 analyst on duty
The size of the current alert backlog in the queue
Legal and contractual rules for that kind of data
The personal preference of the handler on duty that day

explanation: Notification duties come from regulations and contracts that attach to the type of data. An initial severity label, workload and personal preference do not create or remove them.

stem: A CSIRT suspects an insider is stealing trade secrets. Before contacting law enforcement, whom should the incident lead consult?

options.text: The suspect's direct manager, who may decide alone
Public relations, who handle all external referral requests
The help desk, who track employee reports
Legal counsel, who advises on involving authorities

explanation: Legal counsel guides referral to authorities and protects evidence and the case. A manager close to the suspect could compromise the matter, public relations manage messaging, and the help desk does not decide referrals.

stem: A Tier 2 analyst needs a suspected infected laptop retrieved from a remote branch but has no physical access there. What is the proper action?

options.text: Close the ticket as out of scope
Escalate to a team with physical access and log the request
Ask the user to mail the laptop in without any handling notes
Hold the ticket until the next scheduled audit

explanation: Needing expertise or physical access beyond the current tier is a reason to escalate, with the request documented. Closing, shipping without records or waiting for an audit leaves the incident unmanaged or damages evidence.

stem: A report timeline merges events from servers in three time zones. What should the author do so the event order is defensible?

options.text: Normalize timestamps to UTC and confirm NTP synchronization
Convert every entry to the headquarters local time only
Sort the entries by the order the logs arrived
Keep each system's own time and note the offsets verbally

explanation: A single reference time plus confirmed clock synchronization makes the sequence of events reliable. Local time alone, arrival order and unrecorded offsets can all misorder events and weaken the report.

stem: When is a lessons learned meeting best held?

options.text: Before containment, to keep team morale high
Soon after closure, while details are fresh
Once a year, alongside the annual security audit
Only after incidents rated critical

explanation: Holding the meeting soon after closure captures accurate memories and keeps momentum for improvements. Before containment, the team is busy responding, a yearly meeting loses detail, and limiting it to critical incidents wastes learning from smaller ones.

stem: A manager wants to show leadership whether the security program is improving. Which presentation of mean time to detect is most useful?

options.text: A single value from the worst incident of the year
A ranking of analysts by their individual speed
A trend across several quarters compared with a target
A count of how many tools were deployed

explanation: Trends against goals show direction and effectiveness. A single outlier, an individual ranking or a tool count does not demonstrate program improvement.

stem: Which group primarily handles media inquiries during a public incident?

options.text: Public relations
A Tier 1 analyst
The forensic examiner
The network engineer

explanation: Public relations controls external messaging so inquiries get consistent, approved answers. Analysts, examiners and engineers focus on technical work.

stem: A server was breached through an exposed management port. The analyst records "the firewall rule allowed the port" as the cause, then asks why the rule existed and finds no change review process. Which is the root cause?

options.text: The exposed management port
The attacker's scan of the network
The age of the firewall hardware
The missing change review process

explanation: The open port is the immediate cause, but the root cause is the process gap that let an unreviewed rule exist. The scan was only the trigger, and hardware age is unrelated.

stem: Which characteristic makes a KPI robust?

options.text: It is measurable and shows both success and failure
It comes from the default dashboard of a vendor tool
It counts only incidents that ended well
Its definition changes each quarter

explanation: A robust KPI can be measured and reflects results in both directions, tied to organizational goals. Defaults, selective counting and shifting definitions undermine trust and trend value.

stem: Which TWO items belong in an executive summary of an incident report?

options.text: The business impact in plain language
Full packet captures of the attack traffic
Registry keys changed on each host
The current response status and next steps
The hash values of every dropped file

explanation: Executives need impact and status with next steps. Packet captures, registry keys and file hashes are technical evidence that belongs in the detailed sections.

stem: Which THREE sections belong in an after-action report?

options.text: A personal performance rating for each responder
A timeline of events and decisions
A request to purge the related logs from the SIEM
Action items with owners and deadlines
The attacker's personal home address
A formal list of lessons learned

explanation: After-action reports cover the timeline, findings, action items and lessons learned. Rating individuals defeats a non-punitive review, purging logs destroys evidence, and personal attacker details are not part of the report.

stem: A breach of customer personal data will soon become public. Which TWO groups must be part of the communication plan?

options.text: The procurement team
Facilities management
Legal and compliance staff
The software license auditors
Public relations staff

explanation: Legal and compliance decide the obligations, and public relations manage the message to customers and media. Procurement, facilities and license auditors have no part in incident communications.

stem: Which TWO are challenges when using KPIs to describe incident response?

options.text: False positives from automated tracking inflate the counts
Trend lines hide the data behind them from the reviewers who read them
Ineffective collection tools can produce inaccurate data
Only SOC managers may view KPI data
Dashboards must be reprinted every day

explanation: Automated tracking noise and weak collection tools both reduce trust in the numbers. Trends do not hide data, viewing is not restricted to managers, and printing frequency is not a KPI problem.

stem: Which TWO practices protect incident communications?

options.text: Share case details in a company-wide chat room
Use encrypted channels for executive updates
Discuss the incident on public social media
Send status updates to outside parties in plain text email messages
Switch to an out-of-band channel if systems are suspect

explanation: Encryption and an out-of-band fallback protect sensitive updates. Broad chat rooms, public posts and plain text mail expose details to people who should not have them.

stem: Which THREE conditions can explain a high mean time to remediate?

options.text: Dependencies between teams that slow fixes
Fast detection times
Unusually low alert volume across all the monitored systems
Resource gaps in the teams doing the fix
A weak patching process
Excellent employee awareness scores

explanation: Dependencies, resource gaps and weak patching all slow removal of the root cause. Fast detection, low alert volume and good awareness do not lengthen remediation.

stem: Which THREE category labels are commonly used for branches of a fishbone diagram?

options.text: Ticket
Payload
People
Process
Calendar quarter
Technology

explanation: People, process and technology are common branches for grouping causes. Ticket, payload and quarter are not cause categories.

stem: Which TWO situations justify escalating an incident to a higher tier?

options.text: The incident needs expertise the current tier lacks
The response requires physical access the analyst lacks
The alert arrived during the overnight shift of the week
A user instead of a monitoring tool opened the ticket
The affected host runs an older OS

explanation: Missing expertise or access are valid reasons to escalate. The time an alert arrives, who opened the ticket or the age of the OS do not by themselves require escalation.

stem: Which TWO items belong in a shift turnover report?

options.text: Open cases with their current status
The analyst's salary band
Personal notes about coworkers
Raw memory dumps from every host on the network segment
Pending actions for the incoming shift

explanation: Turnover reports carry the operational picture forward. Pay, personal notes and raw dumps are not shift handover content.

stem: Which TWO items are technical details found in a post-incident report?

options.text: The next fiscal year hiring plan for the whole department
The IoC observed during the incident
The affected systems and artifacts
The legal team vacation schedule
The cafeteria menu for the week

explanation: Post-incident reports record indicators, evidence and affected systems. Hiring plans, vacation schedules and menus are unrelated to the incident.

stem: Which TWO are external stakeholders in an incident communication plan?

options.text: Customers
Regulatory agencies
Tier 1 analysts
The internal legal staff
Sales department employees

explanation: Customers and regulators sit outside the organization and receive limited, required information. Analysts, internal legal staff and employees are internal stakeholders.

stem: Put the steps of building an after-action report into the order they are done. Each step needs the output of the step before it.

steps.text: Write findings and recommended improvements into the report
Reconstruct the incident timeline from logs and tickets
Track the action items and report metric trends to leadership
Hold the blame-free lessons learned meeting using the timeline
Assign an owner and due date to each action item

explanation: The timeline gives the lessons learned meeting its facts, the meeting produces the findings written into the report, the findings produce action items to assign, and tracking happens only once owners exist.

partExplanations.0: The timeline comes first because every later step relies on an accurate account of what happened.
partExplanations.1: The meeting reviews the timeline and surfaces what worked and what did not.
partExplanations.2: Findings and recommendations are written up from the meeting.
partExplanations.3: Each recommended action then gets an owner and a due date.
partExplanations.4: Tracking and reporting trends can only follow once the actions have owners.

stem: Put these responders in the order they are first required as incident severity rises, from the lowest severity to the highest.

steps.text: High severity: Tier 3 analysts and specialists lead the response
Low severity: a Tier 1 analyst handles the alert
Critical severity: executives and key support teams are engaged
Medium severity: a Tier 2 analyst investigates the incident

explanation: Escalation follows severity: Tier 1 handles low items, Tier 2 takes medium, Tier 3 and specialists take high, and critical incidents bring in executives and support teams.

partExplanations.0: Low severity items stay with Tier 1 analysts.
partExplanations.1: Medium severity needs the deeper investigation skills of Tier 2.
partExplanations.2: High severity calls for Tier 3 analysts and specialists.
partExplanations.3: Critical severity is escalated to executives and key support teams.

stem: The SOC lead is preparing a metrics slide. Use the table of closed incidents to answer each question.

payload.caption: Closed incidents, minutes after the start of the activity

fields.label: Incident with the longest time to detect

options.text: CASE-1042
CASE-1043
CASE-1044

explanation: Each mean is the column total divided by 4 incidents. Detection: 30 + 90 + 60 + 40 = 220, so 55. Remediation: 240 + 480 + 360 + 120 = 1,200, so 300. Closing: 300 + 540 + 420 + 180 = 1,440, so 360.

partExplanations.mttd: 30 + 90 + 60 + 40 = 220; 220 divided by 4 is 55 minutes. The 50 is the median, not the mean.
partExplanations.slow: CASE-1042 took 90 minutes to detect, more than any other incident.

stem: Match each incident record to what it is used for.

prompts.text: Gives the board a plain-language view of impact and status
Reviews a closed incident with findings and action items
Hands open cases and pending actions to the next shift
Maps observed tactics and indicators so rules can be tuned
Records who handled each item of evidence, and when

explanation: Each record has its own audience and purpose: leaders get the summary, the team gets the after-action review, the next shift gets the turnover report, detection engineers get threat intelligence, and evidence handling is tracked on a custody form.

partExplanations.p1: The executive summary translates findings into business impact for leadership.
partExplanations.p2: An after-action report evaluates the response and lists action items.
partExplanations.p3: A turnover report carries the operational picture across shifts.
partExplanations.p4: Internal threat intelligence turns incident observations into detection improvements.
partExplanations.p5: The chain-of-custody form tracks every handler of evidence.

stem: Sort each security operations metric into what it mainly measures.
explanation: The three mean time metrics are durations averaged across incidents. Alert volume is a count, and the false positive and phishing click rates are proportions.

partExplanations.detect: Mean time to detect is an average duration.
partExplanations.close: Mean time to close is an average duration through documentation.
partExplanations.remed: Mean time to remediate is an average duration to remove the root cause.
partExplanations.alerts: Alert volume is a count over a period.
partExplanations.fpr: The false positive rate is a share of alerts.
partExplanations.click: The click rate is a share of employees who clicked.

stem: Match each audience in the incident communication plan to the message it should receive.

labels.text: Severity, impact and status over a secure channel
Limited notice of affected data and steps to take
Full facts for liability and notification decisions
Required breach notice within the legal deadline
Raw packet captures and tool configurations

explanation: Each audience gets the level of detail it needs: leaders get impact and status, customers get limited facts and actions, counsel gets full facts for legal decisions, and regulators get the notice the law requires.

partExplanations.z1: Leadership needs severity, impact and status, sent securely.
partExplanations.z2: Customers get limited information about their data and what to do.
partExplanations.z3: Counsel needs the full facts to advise on liability and notification.
partExplanations.z4: Regulators receive the required notice by the legal deadline.

stem: The incident queue export for the day is below. Review it, then complete each step.

steps.label: Type a command that lists every critical ticket in ir_tickets.log
Type a command that counts the tickets whose status is open
CASE-2032 is critical and open, and leadership has not been told. Choose the best next action.

options.text: Brief executives and key support teams over a secure channel, and note it in the ticket
Wait for the Tier 3 analyst to close it, then include it in the monthly report
Lower the severity to high so the on-call queue stays short
Publish a press statement before the facts are confirmed

explanation: grep filters the export to matching lines, and `-c` or `wc -l` counts them. A critical ticket with no leadership notice needs executives and support teams engaged through a secure channel, with the step recorded; waiting, downgrading or going public early are all wrong.

partExplanations.crit: grep critical ir_tickets.log prints CASE-2032 and CASE-2036.
partExplanations.count: grep -c status=open ir_tickets.log reports 4: CASE-2032, CASE-2033, CASE-2035 and CASE-2037.
partExplanations.act: Critical incidents are escalated to executives and key support teams, using a secure channel and a record in the ticket.
